title: Hackers heated French supermarket fridges to 50 °C

ticker: Paris prosecutors open an investigation into the attack on supermarket refrigeration
CERT-FR: attacks on refrigeration controllers are probably still ongoing
Alert widened on Tuesday to Dixell and Copeland controllers
No claim of responsibility so far

m1.alt: A supermarket chest freezer full of food

m2.alt: Food thrown into a supermarket dumpster

m3.alt: An Intermarché supermarket in Vonnas, France

m4.alt: Dominique Schelcher, CEO of Coopérative U

scenes.heading: Hackers heated supermarket fridges to *50 °C*
scenes.narration: Overnight into Monday, hundreds of French supermarkets lost their cold. Nobody broke in. Someone, over the internet, pushed fridges and freezers to fifty degrees Celsius. How is that even possible?

scenes.title: The morning after
scenes.narration: On Monday morning, staff found warm freezers and spoiled stock. Fresh and frozen food had to be thrown away. And according to Paris prosecutors, some equipment caught fire.

scenes.title: Stores hit
scenes.narration: The count is still moving. Intermarché's owner says about one hundred fifty to one hundred eighty of its stores, other reports say three hundred. Carrefour said eighty. U, eighty, its boss says. Monoprix, around thirty. E.Leclerc, several.

scenes.title: Across France
scenes.narration: It was nationwide. An Intermarché in La Haye, in Normandy, said its cases hit eighty degrees. In Alsace, two stores reported about two hundred seventy thousand euros in losses.

scenes.title: How do you hack a fridge?
scenes.narration: Big stores run their cold cases from one central controller. Maintenance companies reach it over the internet. The attackers reached these controllers remotely too, and switched the cases into defrost mode.

scenes.title: Defrost, stretched
scenes.narration: Defrosting is normal. Heaters melt the ice for a short while, and alarms expect it. In some stores, according to Le Monde, cycles were stretched from one hour to eight, to delay the alarms. Meanwhile, the food warmed up.

scenes.title: Why these machines
scenes.narration: Most of the controllers hit are made by Danfoss, a Danish company. Danfoss says most were old models that no longer get security updates. Some newer ones ran outdated software. On Tuesday, the alert grew to two more brands, Dixell and Copeland.

scenes.title: Reactions

quotes.text: Targeting this equipment is of extreme gravity, and unprecedented.
Tens of millions of euros nationwide, in a single day.

scenes.narration: The head of Coopérative U said targeting this equipment is of extreme gravity, and unprecedented. Intermarché's boss spoke of tens of millions of euros in losses nationwide, a figure not verified yet.

scenes.title: How it unfolded

items.text: Researchers publish flaws in a *Danfoss* controller, already patched
Cyber agency alert · Paris investigation opens

scenes.narration: The warnings came first. In August, researchers published flaws in a Danfoss controller, flaws that updates had fixed. In September, Danfoss flagged another. Then came the night of October eleventh. On Monday, the national cyber agency issued an alert, and Paris prosecutors opened an investigation.

scenes.title: Still unknown
scenes.narration: And it may not be over. The agency warns attacks are probably still going on. We still don't know who did it, since nobody has claimed it. Or exactly how they got in. Or the final bill.

scenes.title: What stores are told

items.text: Access only via a *secure private link*

scenes.narration: The agency's advice is direct. Take these controllers off the internet, and reach them only through a secure private link. Update them, and change default passwords. Old, exposed units are very likely compromised already.

scenes.title: The question
scenes.narration: No data theft has been reported. The damage was physical: heat, spoiled food, fires. So, should equipment like this be online at all? Tell me in the comments.

scenes.title: Sources
scenes.narration: Sources are on screen and in the description.

notes: Nobody has claimed the attack. Do not attribute it: security researcher Bluetouff warned that blaming a country without evidence is premature (MacGeneration).

Store counts are provisional and differ by source: Les Mousquetaires told Reuters about 150 and TIME about 180 stores; AFP and BFM TV reported at least 300 Intermarché/Netto stores. Coopérative U: 'at least 100' (TIME), 80 per its CEO on Tuesday (AFP). Monoprix: about 30 (AFP), about 5% of its stores (Reuters).

La Haye (Normandy): an Intermarché said on Facebook its cases reached 80 °C (reported by TIME). Haguenau (Alsace): two stores, about €270,000 in losses (La Dépêche via MacGeneration; BFM TV via TIME says 'Alsace').
Danfoss: AK-SM 800 is end of life since May 2021, AK-SC 355 phased out in 2016; neither gets security updates. Some AK-SM 800A units on outdated firmware were also hit (Danfoss via Reuters/CBS).

CERT-FR updated its alert on 13 October to add Dixell xweb and Copeland xweb, and says attack campaigns are probably still ongoing. An E.Leclerc in the Tarn using Dixell regulators reported a cold-chain break on Tuesday; a link with the Danfoss cases is not established.

CERT-FR advice: remove internet exposure, restore access only through a secure VPN or protected network (IP filtering only as an emergency measure), check defrost schedules, update firmware, enable Danfoss 'Strict' security, change default passwords; for compromised units, factory reset and reconfigure (a reset alone is not enough). End-of-life units exposed online have a very high probability of compromise.
Exposure is not compromise: scan data (U.K. Cyber Defence via TIME) found France held nearly 60% of exposed Danfoss controllers; a reachable controller is not necessarily a hacked one.

Reuters cited a Sekoia analyst saying stores in Spain, Portugal, Poland, Germany and Belgium may also be affected; none confirmed. Ahold Delhaize reported a separate cybersecurity incident the same day; no link established.

Intermarché told AFP some insurance contracts may not cover this kind of incident. U's CEO said only a minority of its 80 stores threw stock away: tens of thousands of euros in a small store, €180,000–200,000 in a hypermarket.
Photos are illustrative (Wikimedia Commons, public domain or CC BY-SA 4.0): they do not show stores confirmed as affected.

publish.description: Overnight on 11–12 October 2026, attackers remotely forced refrigeration in hundreds of French supermarkets into defrost mode, up to 50 °C. Food was thrown away and some equipment caught fire. What happened, how it worked, and what is still unknown, as of 13 October.
